claim: Tribolium castaneum has emerged as a model for brain development and evolution.
source: Tribolium castaneum (Tribolium hereafter) has been introduced as an additional model for insect neural development (Biffar and Stollewerk, 2014; Biffar and Stollewerk, 2015; Koniszewski et al., 2016; Posnien et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work establishing Tribolium as a model system

claim: Nine type II neuroblast lineages per hemisphere were found in the Tribolium embryo.
source: Intriguingly, we found nine lineages per hemisphere in the Tribolium embryo while Drosophila produces only eight per brain hemisphere.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Drosophila produces only eight type II neuroblast lineages per brain hemisphere.
source: Intriguingly, we found nine lineages per hemisphere in the Tribolium embryo while Drosophila produces only eight per brain hemisphere.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Drosophila

claim: Embryonic type II neuroblast lineages are significantly larger in Tribolium than in Drosophila.
source: These embryonic lineages are significantly larger in Tribolium than they are in Drosophila and contain more intermediate progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Embryonic type II neuroblast lineages contain more intermediate progenitors in Tribolium than in Drosophila.
source: These embryonic lineages are significantly larger in Tribolium than they are in Drosophila and contain more intermediate progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-otd is absent from all type II neuroblasts and intermediate progenitors.
source: Notably, Tc-otd is absent from all type II neuroblasts and intermediate progenitors, whereas Tc-six3 marks an anterior subset of the type II lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six3 marks an anterior subset of type II neuroblast lineages.
source: Notably, Tc-otd is absent from all type II neuroblasts and intermediate progenitors, whereas Tc-six3 marks an anterior subset of the type II lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six4 specifically marks the territory where anterior-medial type II neuroblasts differentiate.
source: Tc-six4 specifically marks the territory where anterior-medial type II neuroblasts differentiate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The higher number and greater lineage size of embryonic type II neuroblasts in the beetle correlate with a previously described embryonic phase of central complex formation.
source: The higher number and greater lineage size of the embryonic type II neuroblasts in the beetle correlate with a previously described embryonic phase of central complex formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data presented in this work and previous studies

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is one of the best understood models for neurogenesis.
source: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster (Drosophila hereafter) has mostly been used for this purpose, making it one of the best understood models for neurogenesis (Konstantinides et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Drosophila may not be a good representation of insect development in many instances and some processes are derived in the fly lineage.
source: Furthermore, Drosophila may in many instances not be a good representation of insect development and some processes are derived in the fly lineage (Hakeemi et al., 2022; Klingler and Bucher, 2022; Tautz et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Tribolium larvae are more mobile than Drosophila larvae through the use of walking legs.
source: However, compared to Drosophila, the larvae are more mobile through the use of walking legs, which allows them to navigate within or between food sources (Farnworth et al., 2020b; Klingler and Bucher, 2022; Koniszewski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The insect central complex is an anterior, midline spanning neuropile.
source: The insect central complex is an anterior, midline spanning neuropile and constitutes an important brain center for the processing of sensory input, coordination of movement, and navigation (Honkanen et al., 2019; Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The central complex constitutes an important brain center for the processing of sensory input, coordination of movement, and navigation.
source: The insect central complex is an anterior, midline spanning neuropile and constitutes an important brain center for the processing of sensory input, coordination of movement, and navigation (Honkanen et al., 2019; Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Tribolium develops a functional larval central complex during embryogenesis.
source: Between the two insect models Drosophila and Tribolium, a temporal shift in the emergence of central complex neuropile was observed, with Tribolium developing a functional larval central complex during embryogenesis, whereas it develops only at the onset of adult life in Drosophila (Farnworth et al., 2020b; Koniszewski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The central complex develops only at the onset of adult life in Drosophila.
source: Between the two insect models Drosophila and Tribolium, a temporal shift in the emergence of central complex neuropile was observed, with Tribolium developing a functional larval central complex during embryogenesis, whereas it develops only at the onset of adult life in Drosophila (Farnworth et al., 2020b; Koniszewski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The entire insect central nervous system including the brain is produced by neural stem cells called neuroblasts.
source: The entire insect central nervous system including the brain is produced by neural stem cells, the neuroblasts (NBs) (Hartenstein and Stollewerk, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Neuroblasts undergo repeated divisions producing rows of ganglion mother cells, which divide one more time to produce neurons and/or glia.
source: NBs undergo repeated divisions producing rows of ganglion mother cells (GMCs), which divide one more time to produce neurons and/or glia (see Figure 1, top panel).
evidence: Supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Type II neuroblasts were found to prominently contribute to the formation of the central complex in Drosophila and the grasshopper Schistocerca gregaria.
source: Intriguingly, in Drosophila and in the grasshopper Schistocerca gregaria, an NB subtype, the type II NBs, were found to prominently contribute to the formation of the central complex (Boyan and Reichert, 2011; Boyan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Type II neuroblasts generate more offspring by producing intermediate progenitors, which also divide in a stem cell-like fashion.
source: These specific NBs generate more offspring by producing another class of neural precursors, the intermediate progenitors (INPs), which also divide in a stem cell-like fashion (Walsh and Doe, 2017; Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Figure 1, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Intermediate cycling progenitors have been described in vertebrates as radial glia cells, which produce a variety of cell types.
source: Type II NBs and INPs have attracted a lot of attention because intermediate, cycling progenitors have also been described in vertebrates, the radial glia cells, which produce a variety of cell types (Malatesta et al., 2008; Barry et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Brain tumors have been induced from type II neuroblast lineages in Drosophila.
source: In addition, in Drosophila, brain tumors have been induced from type II NB lineages (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005), opening up the possibility of modeling tumorigenesis in an invertebrate brain, thus making these lineages one of the most intriguing stem cell models in invertebrates (Homem and Knoblich, 2012; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The number of neurons produced by each type II neuroblast is significantly larger than the offspring of a type I neuroblast in the developing insect brain.
source: In the developing insect brain, the number of neurons that is produced by each type II NB is significantly larger than the offspring of a type I NB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type II neuroblasts

claim: Medial Drosophila type II neuroblasts produce an average of 450 neurons.
source: Medial Drosophila type II NBs produce an average of 450 neurons, whereas type I NBs of the brain only generate 100–200 neurons each (Bello et al., 2008; Boyan and Williams, 2011; Izergina et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Type I neuroblasts of the Drosophila brain only generate 100–200 neurons each.
source: Medial Drosophila type II NBs produce an average of 450 neurons, whereas type I NBs of the brain only generate 100–200 neurons each (Bello et al., 2008; Boyan and Williams, 2011; Izergina et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Type II neuroblasts and intermediate progenitors are widely believed to be conserved within insects based on descriptions in the grasshopper Schistocerca gregaria.
source: Based on descriptions of large proliferative lineages in the grasshopper S. gregaria, a hemimetabolous insect distantly related to flies, it is widely believed that type II NBs and INPs are conserved within insects (Boyan and Reichert, 2011; Boyan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: A molecular characterization of type II neuroblast lineages has not been performed in an insect other than Drosophila.
source: However, a molecular characterization of such lineages that, on the one hand, will allow to test whether the cell type markers characterized in Drosophila are more widely conserved, and, on the other hand, will facilitate an identification of subcell types, has not been performed in an insect other than Drosophila.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work

claim: The characterization of type II neuroblasts in Drosophila has been based on a specific reporter line in which eGFP expression is driven by an earmuff (fez/erm) enhancer element and marks INP lineages.
source: The characterization of type II NBs in Drosophila has in large parts been based on a specific reporter line in which eGFP expression is driven by an earmuff (fez/erm) enhancer element and marks INP lineages (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Pfeiffer et al., 2008; Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The ETS-transcription factor pointed (pnt) marks type II neuroblasts in Drosophila.
source: The ETS-transcription factor pointed (pnt) marks type II NBs (Xie et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2011), which do not express the type I NB marker asense (ase) but the neural gene deadpan (dpn) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Type II neuroblasts do not express the type I neuroblast marker asense (ase) but express the neural gene deadpan (dpn).
source: The ETS-transcription factor pointed (pnt) marks type II NBs (Xie et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2011), which do not express the type I NB marker asense (ase) but the neural gene deadpan (dpn) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Intermediate progenitors express fez/erm and ase and at a more mature stage also dpn.
source: INPs express fez/erm and ase and at a more mature stage also dpn, whereas prospero (pros) marks mature INPs and GMCs (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Prospero (pros) marks mature intermediate progenitors and ganglion mother cells.
source: INPs express fez/erm and ase and at a more mature stage also dpn, whereas prospero (pros) marks mature INPs and GMCs (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Bayraktar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Six4 is a marker for Drosophila type II neuroblasts and intermediate progenitors.
source: Six4 is another marker for Drosophila type II NBs and INPs (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: A CRISPR-Cas9-induced genome editing was used to create a Tc-fez/erm enhancer trap line.
source: To that end, we used CRISPR-Cas9-induced genome editing for creating a Tc-fez/erm enhancer trap line to characterize embryonic Tc-fez/erm-expressing cells, including INPs and GMCs of type II NB lineages, and combined this line with other labeling methods, including multicolor hybridization chain reaction (HCR) (Choi et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in this study

claim: The Tribolium embryo produces nine Tc-pnt-expressing type II neuroblasts compared to only eight type II neuroblast lineages in the Drosophila embryo.
source: We found that the Tribolium embryo produces nine Tc-pnt-expressing type II NBs compared to only eight type II NB lineages in the Drosophila embryo (Álvarez and Díaz-Benjumea, 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Type II neuroblast lineages produce central complex cells.
source: We show that these lineages produce central complex cells and confirm a largely conserved molecular code that differentiates INPs of distinct maturation stages and GMCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: A largely conserved molecular code differentiates intermediate progenitors of distinct maturation stages and ganglion mother cells.
source: We show that these lineages produce central complex cells and confirm a largely conserved molecular code that differentiates INPs of distinct maturation stages and GMCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Lineage sizes in Tribolium embryos are considerably larger and include more mature intermediate progenitors than in the Drosophila embryo.
source: Intriguingly, we found that lineage sizes in Tribolium embryos are considerably larger and include more mature INPs than in the Drosophila embryo (Álvarez and Díaz-Benjumea, 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The placodal marker gene Tc-six4 characterizes the embryonic tissue that gives rise to the larger anterior group of type II neuroblasts.
source: We also show that the placodal marker gene Tc-six4 characterizes the embryonic tissue that gives rise to the larger anterior group of type II NBs, whereas Tc-six3 is marking only an anterior subset of these lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six3 marks only an anterior subset of type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We also show that the placodal marker gene Tc-six4 characterizes the embryonic tissue that gives rise to the larger anterior group of type II NBs, whereas Tc-six3 is marking only an anterior subset of these lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: There is a part of the central complex precursors expressing neither Tc-six3 nor Tc-otd.
source: Interestingly, there is a part of the central complex precursors expressing neither Tc-six3 nor Tc-otd, which is absent from all type II NB lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The reporter construct was inserted 160 bp upstream of the fez/erm-transcription start site using the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair mechanism.
source: The reporter construct was inserted 160 bp upstream of the fez/erm-transcription start site using the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair mechanism (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A for scheme).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in this study

claim: At the embryonic stage fez-mm-eGFP co-localized with most Tc-fez/erm-expressing cells in an area that will give rise to the protocerebral structures mushroom bodies, larval eyes, and central complex.
source: We found that at the embryonic stage fez-mm-eGFP co-localized with most Tc-fez/erm-expressing cells in an area that will give rise to the protocerebral structures mushroom bodies, larval eyes, and central complex (Posnien et al., 2023; Posnien et al., 2011b; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: A total of nine Tc-pnt and Tc-fez/erm-expressing clusters were found instead of the eight expected from flies.
source: We found a total of nine such clusters instead of the eight expected from flies (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: The large Tc-pnt-expressing cells and fez-mm-eGFP-expressing cells are mitotically active.
source: We also found that the large Tc-pnt-expressing cells as well as fez-mm-eGFP-expressing cells are mitotically active (Figure 3C–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Seven Tc-pnt-clusters are present in a horse-shoe-shaped formation surrounding fez-mm-eGFP-positive cells at stage NS11.
source: At stage NS11, seven Tc-pnt-clusters are present in a horse-shoe-shaped formation surrounding fez-mm-eGFP-positive cells (white arrows in Figure 3A, star marks one cluster out of focus).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: At stage NS13, the number of Tc-pnt-clusters has increased to nine.
source: At stage NS13, these groups are found in a position at the medial border of the head lobes and their number has increased to nine.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: The nine type II neuroblast clusters are assigned into two groups: one anterior median group consisting of seven type II neuroblasts and one posterior group consisting of two type II neuroblasts.
source: Based on their position by the end of embryogenesis (stage NS14), we assign the nine type II NB clusters into two groups: one anterior median group consisting of seven type II NBs and one posterior group consisting of two type II NBs (see Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: The cells assigned as type II neuroblasts had a significantly larger diameter (av.: 12.98 µm; n=43) than cells of the reference sample (av.: 6.75 µm; n=1579).
source: We found that the cells that we had assigned as type II NBs had a significantly larger diameter (av.: 12.98 µm; n=43) than cells of the reference sample (av.: 6.75 µm; n=1579) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The diameters of nuclei of type II neuroblasts were significantly larger (av.: 8.73 µm; n=17) than the ones of a control sample (av.: 5.21 µm; n=1080).
source: We also found that the diameters of nuclei of type II NBs were significantly larger (av.: 8.73 µm; n=17) than the ones of a control sample (av.: 5.21 µm; n=1080) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The large Tc-pnt-positive but fez-mm-eGFP-negative cells (i.e., type II neuroblasts) express the gene Tc-dpn.
source: We found that the large Tc-pnt-positive but fez-mm-eGFP-negative cells (i.e., type II NBs) express the gene Tc-dpn, in line with expression of this gene in Drosophila neural precursors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tribolium type II neuroblasts do not express Tc-ase.
source: Like Drosophila type II NBs, these cells do not express the type I NB marker Tc-ase (Figure 5D, yellow arrowhead).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Expression of Tc-ase starts in immature Tc-pnt-positive intermediate progenitors.
source: Expression of Tc-ase starts in the following in immature Tc-pnt-positive INPs (Figure 5D , blue arrowhead) and is maintained in INPs that are Tc-pnt-negative but are marked by fez-mm-eGFP (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-dpn is absent from immature Tc-pnt-positive intermediate progenitors but is expressed in mature intermediate progenitors.
source: Tc-dpn is absent from immature Tc-pnt-positive INPs (Figure 5D, pink arrowhead) but is expressed in mature INPs (Figure 5B, orange arrowheads).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Cells that are located at the distal end of the lineages that do not express Tc-dpn but are positive for fez-mm-eGFP and Tc-ase are classified as ganglion mother cells.
source: Cells that are located at the distal end of the lineages that do not express Tc-dpn but are positive for fez-mm-eGFP and Tc-ase are classified as GMCs (Figure 5B, C and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-pros is expressed in most fez-mm-eGFP expressing cells of a lineage.
source: We found the gene Tc-pros expressed in most fez-mm-eGFP expressing cells of a lineage (in Figure 6A and B) and infer from the extent of the expression that it is expressed in mature INPs (Tc-dpn+) and GMCs (Tc-dpn-).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Fez-mm-eGFP-positive cells at the base of the lineage that do not express Tc-pros are immature intermediate progenitors.
source: Fez-mm-eGFP-positive cells at the base of the lineage that do not express Tc-pros are immature INPs (Figure 6A and B, blue arrowheads).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The expression dynamics found in the Tribolium type II neuroblast lineages are very similar to the one found in Drosophila.
source: In summary, the expression dynamics found in the Tribolium type II NB lineages are very similar to the one found in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Immature-I and -II intermediate progenitors are not dividing, whereas mature intermediate progenitors are.
source: Image stacks from specimens co-stained with the anti-PH3 mitosis marker (data shown in Figure 3C and listed in Tables 1 and 2, available at https://doi.org/10.25625/8IVICL) indicate that immature-I and -II INPs are not dividing, whereas mature INPs are.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: The skh-positive cells are located directly distally of the type II neuroblast lineages in a position where the type II neuroblasts-derived neural cells are expected.
source: By co-staining for Tc-pnt and Tc-fez/erm RNA in the background of the skh-line, we found that the skh-positive cells are located directly distally of the type II NB lineages in a position where the type II NBs-derived neural cells are expected (Figure 8A, B, E and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: At the transition between Tc-fez/erm and skh cells some cells express both markers.
source: Most skh-cells have switched off fez/erm-expression, but at the transition between Tc-fez/erm and skh cells we found some cells that express both markers (Figure 8D and E), supporting the view that many skh-positive central complex cells stem from the fez-expressing GMCs of the type II NB lineages (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Both the anterior-median group and the posterior group of type II neuroblast lineages contribute to central complex neuropile.
source: We found skh cells at the end of lineages of the anterior-median group (Figure 8A) and at the end the two posterior lineages (Figure 8B). We therefore conclude that both groups contribute to central complex neuropile (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: In beetles, a single-unit central body develops during embryogenesis and has gained functionality at the onset of larval life.
source: In beetles, a single-unit central body (most likely constituting the fan-shaped body; Koniszewski et al., 2016) develops during embryogenesis and has gained functionality at the onset of larval life (Farnworth et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: In Drosophila central complex commissural tracts originating from type II neuroblasts form in the embryo but the type II neuroblasts become quiescent and only resume divisions in the late larval stage.
source: By contrast, in Drosophila central complex commissural tracts originating from type II NBs form in the embryo but the type II NB become quiescent and only resume divisions in the late larval stage (Walsh and Doe, 2017; Álvarez and Díaz-Benjumea, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: A functional central complex is only observed in the adult fly.
source: In stark contrast to Tribolium, a functional central complex is only observed in the adult fly (Farnworth et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The volume of the L1 central brain including the central complex is about four times larger in Tribolium than it is in Drosophila.
source: In addition, the volume of the L1 central brain including the central complex is about four times larger in Tribolium than it is in Drosophila (Bullinger, 2024), while there are only small differences in the relative neuropilar volumes of the adult beetle and fly central bodies (Bullinger, 2024; Dreyer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: There are only small differences in the relative neuropilar volumes of the adult beetle and fly central bodies.
source: In addition, the volume of the L1 central brain including the central complex is about four times larger in Tribolium than it is in Drosophila (Bullinger, 2024), while there are only small differences in the relative neuropilar volumes of the adult beetle and fly central bodies (Bullinger, 2024; Dreyer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: At stage NS13 (early retracting embryo) each lineage consisted on average of 18.4 progenitor cells and at stage NS14 (retracted embryo) of 16.8 progenitors.
source: We found that at stage NS13 (early retracting embryo) each lineage consisted on average of 18.4 progenitor cells and at stage NS14 (retracted embryo) of 16.8 progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Between 5 and 10% of the cells in type II neuroblast lineages were marked by the PH3 antibody.
source: Between 5 and 10% of the cells were marked by the PH3 antibody.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The beetle lineages were significantly larger than the corresponding ones in Drosophila.
source: We found that the beetle lineages were significantly larger than the corresponding ones in Drosophila (Figure 9; Drosophila data taken from Walsh and Doe, 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The embryonic type II neuroblast lineages in Tribolium comprised significantly more mature intermediate progenitors (Tc-dpn+/ Tc-fez+) than the corresponding lineages in Drosophila.
source: We also found that the embryonic type II NB lineages in Tribolium comprised significantly more mature INPs (Tc-dpn+/ Tc-fez+) than the corresponding lineages in Drosophila (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The higher numbers of progenitor cells in Tribolium compared to Drosophila correlate with a previously described earlier (i.e., embryonic) formation of a functional central complex in beetles.
source: The described observations on the higher numbers of progenitor cells in Tribolium compared to Drosophila correlate with a previously described earlier (i.e., embryonic) formation of a functional central complex in beetles, which is present in the first larval stage (Farnworth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in this work and previous studies

claim: Tc-otd was not co-expressed with fez-mm-eGFP marked cells of both the anterior-medial and posterior lineages.
source: We found no co-expression of fez-mm-eGFP marked cells of both the anterior-medial and posterior lineages with Tc-otd.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-otd was absent from the type II neuroblasts themselves.
source: Tc-otd was also absent from the type II NBs themselves (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six4 is expressed specifically in that area of the head lobe in which the type II neuroblasts clusters 1–6 of the anterior-medial group first differentiate.
source: Interestingly, we found that Tc-six4 is expressed specifically in that area of the head lobe in which the type II NBs clusters 1–6 of the anterior-medial group first differentiate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: At stage NS13, Tc-six4 marks both type II neuroblasts and fez-mm-eGFP-expressing intermediate progenitors and some surrounding cells.
source: At stage NS13, Tc-six4 marks both, type II NBs and fez-mm-eGFP-expressing INPs and some surrounding cells (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: At stage NS14, Tc-six4 still marks the type II neuroblasts clusters of the anterior-medial group but is not expressed in the fez-mm-eGFP intermediate progenitors.
source: At the following differentiation stage (NS14), Tc-six4 still marks the type II NBs clusters of the anterior-medial group but is not expressed in the fez-mm-eGFP INPs (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six4 is not expressed in the posterior group of type II neuroblasts but only marks type II neuroblasts of the anterior-medial group.
source: It is also not expressed in the posterior group of type II NBs but only marks type II NBs of the anterior-medial group.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Tc-six3 marks, and is restricted to, the anterior-most lineages 1–4, including both the type II neuroblasts and the fez-mm-eGFP marked intermediate progenitors/ganglion mother cells.
source: Finally, we found that Tc-six3 marks, and is restricted to, the anterior-most lineages 1–4, including both the type II NBs and the fez-mm-eGFP marked INPs/GMCs (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: A total of nine type II neuroblast lineages on each side of the Tribolium embryonic head were identified.
source: We have identified a total of nine type II NB lineages on each side of the Tribolium embryonic head.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work presented in this manuscript

claim: Only eight embryonic type II neuroblasts were identified in both the hemimetabolan grasshopper Schistocerca gregaria and the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster.
source: This represents a major evolutionary divergence as in both the hemimetabolan grasshopper S. gregaria and the fruit fly D. melanogaster only eight embryonic type II NBs were identified (Walsh and Doe, 2017; Boyan and Williams, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The finding of an additional type II neuroblast lineage at the embryonic stage shows that the number of type II neuroblasts is not fixed across insects.
source: Our finding of an additional type II NB lineage at the embryonic stage shows that the number of type II NBs is not fixed across insects and suggests that evolutionary divergence in brain development between species may be driven by differences in the number of progenitor lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of this study

claim: Evolutionary divergence in brain development between species may be driven by differences in the number of progenitor lineages.
source: Our finding of an additional type II NB lineage at the embryonic stage shows that the number of type II NBs is not fixed across insects and suggests that evolutionary divergence in brain development between species may be driven by differences in the number of progenitor lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings of this study

claim: In Schistocerca, there is no obvious clustering of type II neuroblasts, and they are all arranged in one row at the medial rim of the head lobes.
source: In the hemimetabolan Schistocerca, there is no obvious clustering of type II NBs, and they are all arranged in one row at the medial rim of the head lobes.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from previous studies

claim: In Tribolium, type II neuroblasts are arranged into two groups per side, one large anterior-medial group containing seven type II neuroblast clusters and one posterior group of two type II neuroblasts.

claim: In Drosophila, there are three described groups of type II neuroblasts referred to as the anterior, the middle, and the posterior clusters.
source: In Drosophila, there are three described groups referred to as the anterior, the middle, and the posterior clusters (Walsh and Doe, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The posterior cluster in Drosophila consists of two type II neuroblasts and most likely corresponds to the posterior two type II neuroblasts in Tribolium.
source: The posterior cluster consists of two type II NBs and therefore most likely corresponds to the posterior two type II NBs in Tribolium.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the data from this study with published work

claim: The Drosophila middle and anterior clusters are most likely equivalent to the anterior-medial group of Tribolium.
source: The Drosophila middle and anterior clusters are most likely equivalent to the anterior-medial group of Tribolium.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the data from this study with published work

claim: There is a tendency toward grouping of type II neuroblasts into subsets in the holometabolan models that was not observed in the only hemimetabolan studied so far.
source: In summary, there is a tendency toward grouping of type II NBs into subsets in the holometabolan models that was not observed in the only hemimetabolan studied so far.

claim: A ninth type II neuroblast was only found in the Tribolium embryo that represents a striking developmentally divergent feature.
source: A ninth type II NB was only found in the Tribolium embryo that represents a striking developmentally divergent feature, but its role and the homologization of individual type II NBs between the different insects require further studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of this study

claim: The results show a large degree of conservation of expression and probably also function of genes defining the different stages of differentiation in type II neuroblast lineages between fly and beetle.
source: Our results show a large degree of conservation of expression and probably also function – at least in holometabola.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: In Drosophila, Pnt suppresses Ase in type II neuroblasts and promotes the formation of intermediate progenitors.
source: In Drosophila, both these factors have key functions in defining the developmental potential of type II NBs and INPs: Pnt suppresses Ase in type II NBs and promotes the formation of INPs (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Loss of pnt expression leads to a de-differentiation of intermediate progenitors as fez/erm is no longer repressed in young intermediate progenitors.
source: Loss of pnt expression leads to a de-differentiation of INPs as fez/erm is no longer repressed in young INPs (Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Fez/Erm controls proliferation of intermediate progenitors by activating Pros and prevents dedifferentiation of intermediate progenitors into type II neuroblasts.
source: Fez/Erm controls proliferation of INPs by activating Pros and prevents dedifferentiation of INPs into type II NBs (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: In Tribolium intermediate progenitors undergo a maturation process, during which expression of Tc-pnt stalls and expression of Tc-fez/erm is switched on.
source: We show that also in Tribolium INPs undergo a maturation process, during which expression of Tc-pnt stalls and expression of Tc-fez/erm is switched on.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: A small window of overlap of Tc-pnt and Tc-fez/erm expression was observed in immature-II intermediate progenitors, highly suggestive of a conserved role of Pnt in the activation of fez/erm.
source: Despite both factors characterizing different stages of INP maturation, they are not completely mutually exclusive and we observed a small window of overlap in immature-II INPs, highly suggestive of a conserved role of Pnt in the activation of fez/erm (Xie et al., 2016; Figure 12).
evidence: This is a primary finding from gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript and an inference about conserved function

claim: Drosophila dpn is a neural marker expressed in type II neuroblasts and again in mature intermediate progenitors, leaving a gap of expression in immature-I and II intermediate progenitors.
source: Drosophila dpn is a neural marker (Bier et al., 1992) expressed in type II NBs and again in mature INPs, leaving a gap of expression in immature-I and II INPs.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Drosophila ase is repressed in type II neuroblasts but expressed together with fez/erm in intermediate progenitors and ganglion mother cells where its expression overlaps with pros.
source: Drosophila ase is repressed in type II NBs but expressed together with fez/erm in INPs and GMCs where its expression overlaps with pros (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Identical dynamics of gene expression were found in Tribolium as in Drosophila, suggesting conservation of gene function within the lineages and a conserved process of intermediate progenitor maturation.
source: We found identical dynamics of gene expression in Tribolium (see Figure 12), suggesting conservation of gene function within the lineages and a conserved process of INP maturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Expression of the genes examined in this study in type II neuroblasts and their lineages is highly conserved in fly and beetle, which is implicit of conserved gene function and a conserved process of central complex formation.
source: In conclusion, expression of the genes examined in this study in type II NBs and their lineages is highly conserved in fly and beetle, which is implicit of conserved gene function and a conserved process of central complex formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: In Tribolium, parts of the central complex develop during embryogenesis and become functional at the onset of the first larval stage.
source: In Tribolium, parts of the central complex develop during embryogenesis. It becomes functional at the onset of the first larval stage and is presumably required for the more complex movements of the beetle larvae using legs (Farnworth et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The functional central complex in Tribolium is presumably required for the more complex movements of the beetle larvae using legs.
source: It becomes functional at the onset of the first larval stage and is presumably required for the more complex movements of the beetle larvae using legs (Farnworth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from published work

claim: In both Drosophila and Tribolium, the anterior groups of type II neuroblasts are fully present in the last third of embryogenesis, with the beginning of germ band retraction.
source: In both Drosophila and Tribolium, the anterior groups of type II NBs (anterior-medial group of Tribolium and anterior and middle cluster of Drosophila) are fully present in the last third of embryogenesis, with the beginning of germ band retraction (Biffar and Stollewerk, 2014; Walsh and Doe, 2017; Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: In the Drosophila embryo, only a limited number of intermediate progenitors and ganglion mother cells are produced before they enter a resting stage prior to hatching.
source: However, in the Drosophila embryo, only a limited number of INPs and GMCs are produced before they enter a resting stage prior to hatching (Walsh and Doe, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The increased activity of type II neuroblast lineages in Tribolium may contribute to the embryonic development of a functional central body and protocerebral bridge.
source: We believe that this increased activity may contribute to the embryonic development of a functional central body and protocerebral bridge (Farnworth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented in this work and previous studies

claim: The hypothesis that increased type II neuroblast activity contributes to embryonic central complex development requires further confirmation by lineage-tracing experiments and testing how manipulating central genes acting within the lineages will affect the timing of central complex development.
source: This hypothesis does however require further confirmation by lineage-tracing experiments and testing how manipulating central genes acting within the lineages will affect the timing of central complex development.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needed to test the hypothesis

claim: Type II neuroblast lineages are much larger in the third larva of Drosophila and contain more intermediate progenitors than the Tribolium embryonic lineages.
source: After preformation in the embryo Drosophila, type II NBs have their main period of activity in the third larva and the lineages are much larger and contain more INPs than the Tribolium embryonic lineages (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013).

claim: The different type II neuroblast lineages contribute to different parts of the brain.
source: The different type II NB lineages contribute to different parts of the brain.

source: For instance, only the anterior four type II NB lineages form the w, x, y, and z tracts of the central complex in flies and grasshoppers.

source: In the ventral nerve cord, the different identities of the NBs are specified by the combination of spatial patterning genes expressed in the neuroectoderm at the time of delamination (Stollewerk, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: In Tribolium, the domains of head patterning genes in the brain neuroectoderm are well characterized and some highly conserved territories like the anterior-medial six3-positive domain were described and suggested to give respective neuroblasts different spatial identities.
source: In Tribolium, the domains of head patterning genes in the brain neuroectoderm are well characterized and some highly conserved territories like the anterior-medial six3-positive domain were described and suggested to give respective NBs different spatial identities (Posnien et al., 2023; Posnien et al., 2011b; Steinmetz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: The Tc-six4 expression domain is largely coincident with an embryonic structure termed insect head placode, a neurogenic, invaginating tissue potentially homologous to the vertebrate adenohypophyseal placode, which is also marked by six4.
source: The Tc-six4 expression domain is also largely coincident with an embryonic structure termed insect head placode, a neurogenic, invaginating tissue (Posnien et al., 2011a; de Velasco et al., 2007) potentially homologous to the vertebrate adenohypophyseal placode, which is also marked by six4 (Posnien et al., 2023; Posnien et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: A placodal origin of Drosophila type II neuroblasts has been shown for one type II neuroblast, and it is assumed that the other type II neuroblasts also stem from placodal tissue.

evidence: Supported by citations to published work

claim: Tc-six4 could contribute to distinguishing the developmental fate of the anterior group of type II neuroblasts from the posterior group.

claim: In the Drosophila larva, Six4 is expressed in all eight lineages where it prevents the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts and a premature differentiation of intermediate progenitors.

claim: The lineages of type II neuroblasts 5 and 6 (and presumably of type II neuroblast 7) of the anterior cluster and the posterior type II neuroblast lineages do neither express Tc-otd nor Tc-six3.
source: Interestingly, the lineages of type II NB 5 and 6 (and presumably of type II NB 7) of the anterior cluster and the posterior type II NB lineages do neither express Tc-otd nor Tc-six3, showing that there are protocerebral structures expressing none of these conserved markers in development, questioning the assigned generalized role of these two factors in subdividing the protocerebrum (Posnien et al., 2023; Steinmetz et al., 2010).
